prompt: A hostname resolves to the expected address, but the TCP connection times out. Explain what is known, what remains open, and your next safe evidence.
directAnswer: DNS resolution is the last proven gate. From the failing namespace, verify source/address-family/route, compare a healthy peer, then use authorized client and both-side transport evidence to distinguish route, neighbor, policy, NAT, delivery, destination response, and return-path failure before changing anything.
foundation: DNS maps a name to records. Routing selects a local path. TCP then attempts transport. Success at one gate does not prove the next.
reasoningSteps: Record exact client, namespace, hostname, returned address, port, connect timer, elapsed time, and cohort.
Confirm application-style resolution and compare a healthy peer.
Read source-address and route selection for the actual address family.
Inspect policy, proxy, VPN, NAT, CNI, and return-path boundaries relevant to that client.
Correlate bounded client timing with destination listener and authorized packet/counter evidence.
Apply one owned reversible fix and verify the original request plus healthy controls.
seniorAnswer: I would not restart DNS because it already returned the expected record for this observation. I would name connect timeout as the first failed gate and preserve the affected namespace. I would compare route/source and policy selection with a healthy peer, then determine whether SYN and reply appear at each owned handoff. If traffic reaches the destination, listener/backlog/host pressure remain; if it does not, I narrow the last observed boundary. Recovery has a prediction, rollback, and end-to-end verification.
weakAnswer: DNS works, so open the firewall everywhere.
whyWeak: It treats unproven policy as cause, expands exposure, ignores route/return/listener/queue alternatives, and has no bounded verification.

evidence.proves: This resolver path returned that address now.
evidence.doesNotProve: Reachability, transport, TLS, HTTP, or another client's cache.

evidence.proves: The local kernel selected those route fields.

evidence.signal: destination sees SYN but client sees no SYN-ACK
evidence.proves: The request reached that capture point and a reply was not observed there/client under the capture limits.
evidence.doesNotProve: Which later return-path boundary lost it without additional evidence.

followUps.answer: Yes, when the named timer covers request or first-byte time rather than only connect; always identify the timer.
